set.explanation: Alcohol is a well-established trigger and risk factor for AF: binge drinking can precipitate paroxysms ('holiday heart'), and regular heavy intake increases AF incidence and recurrence; abstinence reduces recurrence. Chronic excess also causes dilated (not hypertrophic) cardiomyopathy and hypertension rather than hypotension.

set.stem: A 55-year-old woman with no past medical history presents with syncope; her ECG (A) shows advanced AV block, and she has painful red nodules on her shins (B). What is the most likely cause of both the cardiac and skin abnormalities?
set.explanation: Heart block in a middle-aged woman together with erythema nodosum suggests sarcoidosis. Cardiac sarcoid causes granulomatous infiltration of the septum and conduction system, leading to AV block, ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death. Cardiac MRI or FDG-PET supports the diagnosis, and treatment is immunosuppression plus a pacemaker or ICD. Hypothyroidism, SLE and syphilis do not produce this combination.

set.stem: Which abnormality is shown on this 12-lead ECG?
set.explanation: The ECG shows a broad QRS with an rSR' ('M'-shaped) complex in V1–V2 and a wide, slurred S wave in I, aVL, V5 and V6: right bundle branch block. LBBB gives a broad QS or rS in V1 with a notched R in V6, P pulmonale is a tall peaked P wave in II, and S1Q3T3 is a non-specific sign of acute right heart strain.

set.stem: A 21-year-old competitive cyclist, asymptomatic and without syncope, has a resting heart rate of 45/min with occasional pauses up to 2.2 seconds. BP 108/72 mmHg; examination is otherwise normal, and the ECG shows sinus rhythm with PR 128 ms and QRS 80 ms. What advice is appropriate?
set.explanation: High vagal tone in endurance athletes commonly causes sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses under 3 seconds (especially at rest or asleep), first-degree block and Wenckebach block. In an asymptomatic athlete with a normal examination these are physiological and need no further tests or restriction. Pacing is considered only for symptomatic bradycardia or pauses of 3 seconds or more while awake.

After overdrive atrial pacing stops, a normal sinus node resumes within about 1500 ms (corrected recovery time under 525 ms); a pause of 1800 ms indicates a prolonged sinus node recovery time, meaning intrinsic SA node dysfunction. The low intrinsic heart rate after autonomic blockade (propranolol plus atropine) supports this. AV nodal disease would show prolonged AV conduction or block instead.

Extrinsic, reversible causes of SA node dysfunction include hypothermia, hypothyroidism, raised intracranial pressure (Cushing reflex), drugs (beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, lithium, digoxin), hyperkalaemia and high vagal tone. Radiation therapy causes permanent intrinsic fibrosis of the conduction system, as do ageing, infiltration and ischaemia.

Patients with the tachy–brady form of sick sinus syndrome have episodes of AF or flutter and so a real thromboembolic risk. Risk factors are age over 65, previous stroke, valve disease, LV dysfunction and atrial enlargement. Anticoagulation is guided by CHA2DS2-VASc, as in other AF, and a pacemaker alone does not remove the embolic risk.

Decremental conduction means AV nodal conduction slows as it is stimulated faster. It is shown by pacing the atrium at progressively shorter cycle lengths and measuring a lengthening atrium-to-His (AH) interval until Wenckebach block occurs. This protects the ventricles in AF; accessory pathways usually lack it, which is why pre-excited AF is dangerous. Drug effects on conduction time do not demonstrate this intrinsic property.

The AV node and His bundle lie close to the aortic annulus, so oedema, suturing or debridement during aortic valve replacement (and TAVI) can cause AV block. Here there is complete heart block with AV dissociation and a broad escape rhythm on day 1. Many cases recover within days; persistent block beyond about 5–7 days needs a permanent pacemaker. Endocarditis and sarcoid are unlikely this soon.

set.stem: An 82-year-old man has had two episodes of sudden syncope without warning in the past week, one causing facial bruising. During a further 'spell' in clinic, the rhythm strip shown is recorded. What type of block is present, matched to the appropriate management?
set.explanation: The strip shows conducted beats with a constant PR interval followed by sudden non-conducted P waves and a pause, which is Mobitz II (infranodal) second-degree AV block causing Stokes–Adams attacks. It is unpredictable and tends to progress to complete block, so permanent pacing is indicated. Mobitz I (Wenckebach) shows progressive PR lengthening and is usually benign.

Mobitz I block during sleep in an asymptomatic endurance athlete is a normal manifestation of high vagal tone, and it resolves with exercise and atropine. No tests or treatment are needed. Pacing is reserved for symptomatic block, and a grandfather with a pacemaker in old age is not a relevant family history.

The choice of ambulatory monitoring depends on symptom frequency: a 24–48 hour Holter for daily symptoms, an external event recorder or patch for symptoms every few days to weeks (as here, every 2–4 days), and an implantable loop recorder for rare symptoms such as infrequent syncope. EP study is for documented or strongly suspected significant arrhythmia, and the history does not justify reassurance without a diagnosis.

set.stem: A 47-year-old woman with a normal examination and ECG has brief 'flip-flopping' palpitations every few days. Event monitoring shows that the symptoms correspond to atrial premature contractions only. Which statement is true?
set.explanation: Atrial premature complexes are very common, are seen on most prolonged recordings (more often than ventricular ectopics), and in a structurally normal heart they are benign. Reassurance and reducing triggers (caffeine, alcohol, nicotine) are enough; a beta-blocker is used only for troublesome symptoms. Echo or stress testing is only needed if there are features of structural or ischaemic heart disease.

set.stem: An 18-year-old volleyball player with rare palpitations and light-headedness has a normal examination; her ECG shows a PR interval of 60 ms, QRS duration of 140 ms and a delta wave (WPW pattern). Which finding is reassuring that she is at low risk and does not need catheter ablation?
set.explanation: Abrupt disappearance of pre-excitation (loss of the delta wave) during exercise shows that the accessory pathway has a long refractory period and cannot conduct rapidly, so the risk of pre-excited AF degenerating to VF is low. High-risk features are a shortest pre-excited RR interval in AF of 250 ms or less, multiple pathways, symptomatic tachycardia and documented AF; ablation is recommended for symptomatic patients and high-risk athletes.

Rhythm control of recent-onset AF (under 48 hours) can be achieved by DC cardioversion or with drugs: flecainide (no structural heart disease), amiodarone or dofetilide. Adenosine only transiently blocks the AV node; it is useful for diagnosing or terminating AV-node-dependent SVT but does not convert AF and may even provoke it.

set.stem: A 79-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%) and hypertension has no new symptoms; BP 108/56 mmHg, HR 88/min. His rhythm strip is shown. Based on this, he now has a definite (class I) indication for which therapy?
set.explanation: The strip shows atrial fibrillation (or flutter-fibrillation) in a man with heart failure, hypertension, vascular disease and age 75 or more: a CHA2DS2-VASc score of at least 5. Oral anticoagulation with a DOAC or warfarin is therefore a class I recommendation. Aspirin is ineffective for AF stroke prevention, flecainide is contraindicated in structural heart disease, and cardioversion is not required in an asymptomatic, rate-controlled patient.

why: Same idea as arr-0029 (vagal manoeuvres first for a stable narrow-complex tachycardia)

set.explanation: Maintaining sinus rhythm with antiarrhythmic drugs has not improved survival compared with rate control (AFFIRM), recurrence is common (about half within a year), and asymptomatic recurrences are frequent. So anticoagulation should be based on stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) rather than on apparent rhythm success, and should not be stopped just because the patient seems to be in sinus rhythm. Dofetilide must be started in hospital with QT monitoring.

set.stem: A young woman collapses while jogging and is unresponsive, with BP 50 mmHg (palpable) and a heart rate of about 280/min. Her 12-lead ECG is shown. What is the next most appropriate step?
set.explanation: The ECG shows an irregular, very fast broad-complex tachycardia with varying QRS morphology, which is pre-excited AF conducting down an accessory pathway; with haemodynamic collapse it needs immediate electrical cardioversion or defibrillation. AV-nodal blocking drugs (beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, adenosine) can accelerate conduction down the pathway and precipitate VF. Pathway ablation follows.

set.stem: A young woman collapses while jogging (BP 50 mmHg, heart rate about 280/min). Her 12-lead ECG is shown. What is the underlying rhythm?
set.explanation: An irregularly irregular broad-complex tachycardia with beat-to-beat variation in QRS width and very fast rates (shortest RR intervals under 250 ms) is AF conducting antegradely down an accessory pathway. VT is usually regular, atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction is regular at about 300/min, and AVRT or AVNRT are regular re-entrant rhythms.

set.stem: A 67-year-old man was given thrombolysis 3 hours ago for an anterolateral STEMI. His monitor now shows the rhythm strip below. What rhythm does this represent?
set.explanation: A regular broad-complex ventricular rhythm at about 60–110/min without preceding P waves, appearing soon after thrombolysis, is an (accelerated) idioventricular rhythm, a marker of successful reperfusion. It is usually self-limiting and benign. VT is faster (over 120/min), and complete heart block shows independent P waves with a slower escape rhythm.

set.stem: A 47-year-old woman on methadone takes leftover erythromycin for a respiratory infection and develops palpitations and light-headedness. The rhythm strip shows recurrent non-sustained runs of the arrhythmia shown. IV magnesium sulfate 2 g does not stop the episodes, and her potassium is normal. What is the next most appropriate step?
set.explanation: Methadone plus erythromycin has prolonged her QT interval, and the strip shows polymorphic VT with twisting QRS axis (torsades de pointes). After IV magnesium and correcting potassium, recurrent pause-dependent torsades is suppressed by increasing the heart rate with an isoprenaline infusion or temporary overdrive pacing, which shortens the QT. Amiodarone prolongs the QT further, beta-blockers slow the rate, and sustained haemodynamically unstable torsades needs defibrillation.

In a regular broad-complex tachycardia, evidence of AV dissociation (independent P waves, fusion or capture beats) is diagnostic of VT. Other VT clues are a history of MI or structural heart disease, extreme axis deviation, very broad QRS (over 160 ms) and concordance in the chest leads. A typical bundle branch block pattern or slowing with vagal manoeuvres suggests SVT with aberrancy, and an irregular variable rhythm suggests pre-excited AF.

set.stem: An 18-year-old man with no symptoms has an ECG at a pre-university medical showing an irregular rhythm: every QRS is preceded by an identical normal P wave with a constant PR interval, and the rate speeds up with inspiration and slows with expiration. What is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia (the heart rate rises on inspiration and falls on expiration through vagal modulation) is a normal finding, most prominent in the young and fit. Every beat is sinus with normal P waves and PR interval, so no investigation is needed. Ectopic atrial rhythms show different P-wave morphology, and AF lacks P waves.

set.stem: A 22-year-old triathlete with type 1 diabetes is recovering from diabetic ketoacidosis. While she is asleep, the monitor shows bradycardia; the ECG is shown (2:1 AV block with narrow QRS complexes). Where is the block most likely to be?
set.explanation: 2:1 AV block cannot be classified as Mobitz I or II from the strip alone, but in a young athlete asleep, with narrow QRS complexes and (often) Wenckebach periods elsewhere, the block is almost certainly in the AV node and vagally mediated. Infranodal (His–Purkinje) block usually has broad QRS complexes, is not improved by atropine, and needs pacing.

set.stem: A young athlete has 2:1 AV block with narrow QRS complexes while asleep (ECG shown), with the block located in the AV node. What would be expected if IV atropine were given?
set.explanation: Atropine blocks vagal tone at both the SA and AV nodes, so it increases the sinus rate and improves nodal conduction, typically restoring 1:1 conduction when the block is vagally mediated in the AV node. With infranodal block, atropine speeds the sinus rate without improving His–Purkinje conduction and can worsen the block ratio, which is a useful bedside discriminator.

set.explanation: In a patient with a parkinsonian tremor, rhythmic 4–6 Hz tremor artefact on the ECG can mimic atrial flutter, AF or even VT. The regular underlying QRS complexes, visible through the artefact, confirm sinus rhythm, so no anticoagulation, cardioversion or rate control is needed. Recording with the limbs relaxed or the electrodes moved proximally helps.

set.stem: A 68-year-old man with non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, hypertension and an unexplained TIA 6 months ago has felt unwell for 5 days; BP 110/78 mmHg, HR 150/min. His ECG is shown. Two doses of IV metoprolol 5 mg slow the rate to 75/min and he feels better, and ablation is planned. What is the next most appropriate step?
set.explanation: The ECG shows typical atrial flutter (saw-tooth F waves in II, III and aVF) with 2:1 conduction. Flutter carries a thromboembolic risk similar to AF, and his CHA2DS2-VASc score is high (heart failure, hypertension, age, previous TIA), so systemic anticoagulation is needed now and before any cardioversion or ablation. Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is highly effective for typical flutter.

set.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with palpitations. Her ECG (shown) has a short PR interval and delta waves. Where is her accessory pathway likely to be?
set.explanation: The delta-wave polarity localises an accessory pathway: a negative delta wave and predominantly negative QRS in V1 (LBBB-like pattern) indicates a right-sided pathway, whereas a positive delta wave in V1 (RBBB-like) indicates a left-sided pathway; inferior-lead polarity separates anterior from posterior locations. This tracing fits a right free-wall pathway.

A wide-complex ventricular rhythm at 75/min shortly after successful thrombolysis, in a well patient, is accelerated idioventricular rhythm, a benign reperfusion arrhythmia. It usually resolves spontaneously and needs only observation. Suppressing it with antiarrhythmics can remove the escape rhythm, and flecainide is contraindicated after MI.

set.stem: A 73-year-old woman has chest discomfort and a regular pulse of 53/min. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia with intermittent pauses of 3 seconds in which no P wave appears. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Sinus pauses with absent P waves indicate failure of SA node impulse formation or exit (sinus arrest or SA block), which, with sinus bradycardia in an older person, is sick sinus syndrome. First-degree block prolongs the PR interval, Mobitz I and II show P waves that are not conducted, and complete heart block shows P waves dissociated from the QRS complexes.

why: Original stem ('3 seconds between each consecutive P wave') was physiologically inconsistent with a pulse of 53; rewritten to describe sinus pauses
Same idea as arr-0004 (progressive PR prolongation with a dropped beat = Mobitz I)

set.explanation: When vagal manoeuvres fail, IV adenosine is the drug of choice to terminate AV-node-dependent SVT (AVNRT, AVRT). It is given as a rapid 6 mg bolus into a large vein and flush, followed by 12 mg and 18 mg if needed, warning the patient about transient chest tightness and flushing; verapamil is the alternative in asthma. Lidocaine, digoxin, amiodarone and quinidine are not first-line.
